item.mechanism: Dislocation nucleation is initiated at vacancy sites formed by disordered atoms, where vacancy aggregation creates local stress concentrations that exceed the critical threshold for dislocation formation.
item.operating_conditions: Uniaxial tensile loading at 10 K, strain rate 10^9 s^-1, various crystal orientations (<110>, <1-12>, <-111>)
item.supporting_observation: Disordered atoms appeared inside the crystal leading to vacancy defects; dislocations predominantly nucleated at vacancy sites during early plastic deformation.
item.scope_limits: Authors acknowledge other stress-induced mechanisms may have been involved; not tested for polycrystalline structures or different initial defect densities.
item.alternatives_considered: Other stress-induced mechanisms for dislocation nucleation not explicitly detailed but acknowledged as possible.
quotes: disordered atoms appeared inside the crystal, leading to the formation of vacancy defects
We observed that dislocations predominantly nucleated at vacancy sites during the early stages of plastic deformation
vacancies tend to diffuse and cluster in regions of high local stress, leading to lattice distortions that act as favorable sites for dislocation formation

item.mechanism: Elevated temperature intensifies atomic thermal vibrations, weakening atomic bonding forces and lowering the critical resolved shear stress, which facilitates dislocation nucleation and motion, thereby reducing yield strength.
item.operating_conditions: Tensile loading at temperatures 10 K, 300 K, and 600 K, fixed strain rate 10^9 s^-1
item.supporting_observation: Yield strength decreased with increasing temperature; dislocation density decreased at higher temperatures due to enhanced mobility and annihilation.
item.scope_limits: Valid for the simulated temperature range (10-600 K); not tested for temperatures above 900 K where the potential function may not be valid.
item.alternatives_considered: None explicitly stated as competing mechanisms for the temperature effect on yield strength.
quotes: Elevated temperatures intensify atomic thermal vibrations, making it easier for atoms to deviate from their equilibrium positions and facilitating dislocation nucleation and movement
higher temperatures lead to stronger thermal vibrations of the atoms, causing larger deviations from their equilibrium positions

item.mechanism: Higher strain rates increase flow stress by generating higher dislocation densities because dislocations do not have sufficient time to annihilate or rearrange, leading to accumulation and internal resistance.
item.operating_conditions: Tensile loading at 300 K, strain rates 10^8 s^-1, 10^9 s^-1, and 10^10 s^-1
item.supporting_observation: Higher strain rates led to higher dislocation densities and increased flow stress; dislocation accumulation was more pronounced at higher rates.
item.scope_limits: Yield strength was found insensitive to strain rate; mechanism applies to post-yield flow stress and dislocation density evolution.
item.alternatives_considered: Previous studies suggesting strain rate restricts dislocation motion to enhance yield strength, which was not observed here.
quotes: at higher strain rates, dislocation motion and interaction may not keep pace with the deformation process, resulting in more dislocation accumulation and insufficient annihilation
Higher strain rates correspond to instantaneous dislocation density strengthening, which leads to higher flow stress

item.mechanism: Anisotropy in yield strength arises because the <-111> direction aligns with the close-packed (111) planes, requiring higher stress to initiate slip compared to other orientations.
item.operating_conditions: Uniaxial tensile loading at 10 K, strain rate 10^9 s^-1, comparing <110>, <1-12>, and <-111> orientations
item.supporting_observation: The <-111> direction had the highest yield strength and elastic modulus; dislocation nucleation onset strain differed due to atomic packing density.
item.scope_limits: Specific to single crystal FCC structure; does not account for grain boundary effects in polycrystals.
item.alternatives_considered: None explicitly stated as competing mechanisms for the anisotropy origin.
quotes: Since this HEA had a single FCC structure and the close-packed plane was (111), tensile loading along the <-111> direction resulted in the highest yield strength

item.mechanism: Intrinsic and extrinsic stacking faults are generated by the motion of Shockley partial dislocations; ESFs result from two partials moving in opposite directions on the same slip plane.
item.operating_conditions: Tensile loading at 10 K, strain rate 10^9 s^-1, various orientations
item.supporting_observation: Dislocation slip resulted in ISFs and ESFs; regions of dislocation accumulation coincided with stacking fault appearance.
item.scope_limits: Observed in single crystal; HCP atoms were attributed to stacking faults rather than true phase transformation in most cases.
item.alternatives_considered: True FCC-to-HCP phase transformation was considered but ruled out for most HCP atoms, which were identified as stacking faults.
quotes: The slip of dislocations results in the formation of intrinsic stacking faults (ISFs) and extrinsic stacking faults (ESFs)

item.mechanism: Work hardening in the <110> orientation is driven by the proliferation of immobile stair-rod dislocations (1/6<110>) formed by the combination of Shockley partials.
item.system: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn HEA single crystal, specifically <110> orientation
item.operating_conditions: Tensile loading at 10 K, strain rate 10^9 s^-1
item.supporting_observation: The <110> curve showed stress increase after yielding (work hardening); 1/6<110> dislocations were immobile and contributed to strengthening.
item.scope_limits: Specific to the <110> orientation where work hardening was observed; other orientations showed stress oscillations or stabilization.
item.alternatives_considered: None explicitly stated as competing mechanisms for work hardening in this orientation.
quotes: the curve for the <110> direction showed an increase in stress after yielding, indicating the occurrence of work hardening
1/6<110> dislocations were immobile dislocations, and their increasing content contributed to work hardening
Some of the 1/6<110> dislocations were formed by the combination of two 1/6<112> Shockley partial dislocations

item.mechanism: Twinning is not observed because the high twinning nucleation energy in HEAs makes dislocation slip and stacking fault propagation more favorable under the simulated conditions.
item.operating_conditions: Tensile loading at 300 K, strain rates 10^8-10^10 s^-1
item.supporting_observation: No significant deformation twins were observed; authors note previous studies found annealing twins at elevated temperatures.
item.scope_limits: Specific to the simulated strain rates and temperatures; twinning may occur under different conditions (e.g., annealing).
item.alternatives_considered: Annealing twins observed in other FCC HEAs at elevated temperatures; deformation twins considered but deemed unfavorable here.
quotes: It should be noted that no significant deformation twins were observed in our simulations
This is likely to be due to the high twinning nucleation energy typical of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which makes twinning less favorable than dislocation slip
previous experimental studies have reported dense annealing twins in FCC HEAs such as FeNiCoCr and NiCoCr under elevated temperatures

item.mechanism: FCC-to-BCC transformation is thermally activated; higher temperatures reduce the diffusion energy barrier, allowing BCC atoms to appear around disordered regions.
item.operating_conditions: Tensile loading at temperatures up to 600 K
item.supporting_observation: BCC atoms were observed around disordered atoms at higher temperatures; no BCC atoms were observed at lower temperatures.
item.scope_limits: Only observed at elevated temperatures (around 600 K); not a dominant mechanism at room temperature or below.
item.alternatives_considered: None explicitly stated as competing mechanisms for the BCC formation.
quotes: with increasing temperature, BCC atoms were observed around the disordered atoms
This phenomenon occurs because higher temperatures reduce the diffusion energy barrier for the FCC-to-BCC transformation
No BCC atoms were observed in any of the three orientations, indicating that no FCC-to-BCC phase transformation occurred during tensile deformation
